paper_metadata.title: Arline Benchmarks: Automated Benchmarking Platform for Quantum Compilers

summary: This paper presents Arline Benchmarks, an automated benchmarking platform for quantum compilers, and evaluates Qiskit, Pytket, Cirq, and PyZX on random and structured circuits. Key reported results include optimal KAK compression for random two-qubit circuits, strong compiler-dependent behavior on three-qubit and routing benchmarks, and structured-circuit compression ratios such as CF(gc,2Q) = 3.11 for PytketChem and 3.46 for PyZX on UCCSD, while the best composite pipelines achieved final CX counts of 206 (H2), 862 (NH), 147 (call option), and 54 (put option).

experiments.description: Benchmarking of random two-qubit circuits for KAK decomposition / compression on all-to-all connectivity using Qiskit, Pytket, Cirq, and PyZX.

problem_formulation.objective_function: Minimize two-qubit and single-qubit gate counts / circuit depth via compiler optimization and KAK decomposition.

problem_instance.description: Random two-qubit circuits used as compiler benchmarks; KAK-optimal synthesis target.

dataset_specification.description: Random circuits sampled from [CX, U3] with fixed size 150 gates and equal CX/U3 density.

problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: 30 random circuit instances; compare pre/post compression metrics against theoretical KAK optimum.

implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Rebase final circuits to hardware-native gate set; equivalence checked via classical fidelity for small circuits.

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: No quantum advantage claim; this is a compiler benchmark on small synthetic circuits.
limiting_factors: No classical baseline for problem solving

notes: Two-qubit benchmark is explicitly described; hardware is not a physical QPU, so hardware.type is not specified.
Circuit depth not given as a single scalar for the benchmark; only gate counts and compression metrics are reported.
The paper studies compiler performance on random two-qubit circuits and compares against the KAK optimal bound, not against a classical algorithmic baseline.

experiments.description: Benchmarking of random three-qubit circuits for compression / synthesis on all-to-all connectivity using Qiskit, Pytket, Cirq, and PyZX.

problem_formulation.objective_function: Minimize two-qubit and single-qubit gate counts / circuit depth via compiler optimization.

problem_instance.description: Random three-qubit circuits used as compiler benchmarks; compared against theoretical lower bounds for generic SU(8) synthesis.

dataset_specification.description: Random circuits sampled from [CX, U3] with fixed size 150 gates and equal CX/U3 density.

problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: 30 random circuit instances; compare pre/post compression metrics and scaling with input CX count.

implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Rebase final circuits to hardware-native gate set; equivalence checked via classical fidelity for small circuits.

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: No quantum advantage claim; this is a compiler benchmark on small synthetic circuits.
limiting_factors: No classical baseline for problem solving

notes: Three-qubit benchmark is explicitly described; hardware is not a physical QPU, so hardware.type is not specified.
Circuit depth not given as a single scalar for the benchmark; only gate counts and compression metrics are reported.
The paper reports theoretical lower bounds for three-qubit synthesis and compiler performance, not quantum advantage.

experiments.description: Benchmarking of routing/mapping subroutines on random k-regular connectivity graphs and on four real hardware connectivity graphs, using random [CX, U3] circuits.

problem_formulation.objective_function: Minimize routing overhead in gate count and depth under connectivity constraints.
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: SWAP insertion / dynamic remapping / greedy routing to satisfy coupling graph.

problem_instance.description: Random circuits routed on sparse and real-device coupling graphs to measure overhead from connectivity constraints.

dataset_specification.description: Random [CX, U3] circuits with total gate count 300; one random k-regular graph instance per k in the reported sweep.

problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Compare CX count overhead and CX depth overhead across graph degree k and across four hardware architectures.

implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Overhead measured as gate-count and depth ratios after routing/mapping.

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: No quantum advantage claim; this is a routing/mapping benchmark for compiler subroutines.
limiting_factors: No classical baseline for problem solving

notes: The paper reports routing on random k-regular graphs and on four named hardware connectivity graphs; no physical QPU execution is described.
The 16-qubit figure is the smallest explicitly named hardware size in the routing section; the benchmark circuits themselves are not tied to a single fixed qubit count beyond the plotted examples.
The paper compares compiler routing overheads across graph families and hardware connectivities, not quantum vs classical computation.

experiments.description: Compression benchmarking of random circuits on all-to-all connectivity: low-density [CX, U3], high-density [CX, U3], and phase-polynomial [CX, Rz] circuits.

problem_formulation.objective_function: Minimize gate count, depth, and hardware cost function under all-to-all connectivity.

problem_instance.description: Synthetic random circuits of three types used to compare compiler compression performance.

dataset_specification.description: 20 random circuit instances per case; total gate count 300 each.

problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Average compression ratios over 20 circuit instances; compare gate-count, depth, and cost-function changes.

hardware.transpilation_target: [CX, U3] or [CX, Rz] with all-to-all connectivity

implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Final circuits rebased to [CX, U3] or equivalent target gate set; classical fidelity used for equivalence checks on small circuits.

notes: This is a compiler benchmark, not a quantum algorithm execution experiment.
The paper reports the Mock IBM All2AIL 10q cost model and gate fidelities; circuit depth is not given as a single scalar.

experiments.description: Benchmarking of structured gate-based quantum algorithms: UCCSD/VQE, Trotterized quantum dynamics, amplitude-estimation option pricing, and Grover search on all-to-all connectivity.

algorithm.variant: UCCSD ansatz for VQE; plus additional structured benchmarks in the same experiment set

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Option pricing benchmark uses amplitude estimation; Grover benchmark uses unstructured search circuit; UCCSD and Trotter benchmarks are direct circuit constructions.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Optimize structured circuits for gate count, depth, and hardware cost after compilation.
problem_formulation.problem_hamiltonian: TFIM Hamiltonian for quantum dynamics benchmark: H = J sum Z_i Z_{i+1} + h sum X_i (and long-range variant).

problem_instance.description: Structured quantum algorithm benchmarks from chemistry, dynamics, finance, and search.
problem_instance.dataset_name: QASM circuits from cited benchmark repository

dataset_specification.description: UCCSD circuits for H2, H2O, LiH, NH, CH; TFIM dynamics circuits for 10/16/20 spins; option pricing via amplitude estimation for European call/put; Grover search instances for 4 and 9-15 qubits.

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: For comparison, circuits are preprocessed to [CX, Rz, Rc] and finally rebased to [CX, U3].
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Compression metrics averaged over several circuit instances per class; compare gate-count, depth, and cost-function changes.

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Preprocess to [CX, Rz, Rc] before final rebasing to [CX, U3].
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Classical fidelity used for equivalence checks on small circuits; final rebasing to hardware-native gate set.

notes: This entry aggregates the structured benchmark suite reported together in Sec. 5.2; the paper does not provide a single unified qubit count, so 11 qubits is the maximum explicitly named among the finance instances (option pricing).
The paper reports multiple structured circuit families; only the gate-based ones are included, and no annealer is present.

experiments.description: Benchmarking of structured quantum circuits for quantum chemistry (UCCSD/VQE), including H2, H2O, LiH, and NH molecules.
key_results: PytketChem and PyZX show the best compression for UCCSD circuits in Fig. 14 and Fig. 18.
Compression ratios for UCCSD circuits reach values such as CF(gc,2Q) = 3.11 for PytketChem and 3.46 for PyZX in Table V.

experiments.description: Benchmarking of Trotterized quantum dynamics circuits for the transverse-field Ising model, including local and long-range interactions.
key_results: ChemPassPl significantly outperforms other frameworks for depth and CX-depth reduction in Fig. 14.
PyZX performs poorly on Trotter circuits, with CF(gc,2Q) = 0.30 in Table V for the original circuits.

experiments.description: Benchmarking of option pricing via amplitude estimation on fully connected hardware.
key_results: PytketChem, Peephole, and Transpile are top performers for option pricing circuits in Fig. 18.
Table V reports CF(gc,2Q) = 0.965 for PytketChem on the original finance benchmark.

experiments.description: Benchmarking of Grover search circuits on fully connected hardware.
key_results: PytketChem is the only subroutine that achieves two-qubit gate count compression for Grover search in Fig. 19.
Table V reports CF(gc,2Q) = 1.19 for PytketChem on original Grover circuits.

experiments.description: Composite pipeline search over five subroutines: EjectPhasedPaulis, Ejectz, FullReduce, Peephole, and Transpile L3.
key_results: Best composite pipelines outperform the best single subroutine for each target circuit class.
Table VII reports final CX counts of 206 (H2), 862 (NH), 147 (call option), and 54 (put option).
